s.defn: The system of producing, distributing, and consuming goods and services in a country.
ex: The market economy uses prices to coordinate production.
A stable economy supports schools and community programs.

s.defn: The careful and efficient use of money and resources to avoid waste.
ex: A school budget teaches economy by planning spending.
Students practice economy by saving paper and energy.

s.defn: The wealth and resources of a country or region; the size and strength of its financial resources.
ex: GDP measures changes in national wealth.
A growing economy increases a country's wealth.

s.defn: To attach or fix one thing to another so that it is held in place.
ex: Students should fasten their seatbelts before the bus moves.
Please fasten the strap around your waist.

s.defn: To close or be closed by a latch or clasp; to fasten with a mechanism that prevents opening.
ex: The door will fasten when the latch engages.
Close the lid so it fastens tightly against spills.

s.defn: A group of things gathered together and kept because they are related or of interest.
ex: The science fair displays a collection of mineral samples from different rocks.
A teacher showed a collection of historical artifacts to illustrate time periods.

s.defn: All items stored and cataloged in a library, museum, archive, or database.
ex: The library collection includes many ancient manuscripts.
Her digital music collection grows as she adds new albums.

s.defn: The act of gathering objects or items for study or enjoyment.
ex: The teacher explained how collecting can teach organization and patience.
A monthly collection project helps learners notice patterns.

s.defn: Fundamental; forming the base level that other ideas build on.
ex: Fundamental skills like addition are the basic building blocks of math.
A basic concept underpins later topics in science.

s.defn: Not elaborate or complicated; plain and easy to understand.
ex: The teacher gave a basic explanation in plain language.
A basic version of the problem was used for review.

s.defn: Relating to a chemical base or alkaline substance.
ex: A basic solution turns blue litmus paper blue.
Sodium hydroxide is a strong base used in labs.

s.defn: The essential elements or fundamentals that form the foundation of a subject.
ex: Students should learn the basics before attempting harder problems.
The basics cover counting, place value, and simple operations.

s.defn: An organism that makes organic matter from sunlight or chemical energy and supplies food and matter for other organisms.
ex: Green plants are producers that use sunlight to make sugar in leaves.
Some bacteria are producers that make organic matter without light.

s.defn: An organism or group in an ecosystem that introduces energy into a food web at the base trophic level.
ex: Producers add energy to the ecosystem for consumers and decomposers.
A pond's producers form the base of its food web.

s.defn: To put into service for a given purpose; to employ or apply something to achieve a result.
ex: The researcher used a standardized protocol to measure the variable.
Participants used calibrated instruments to collect data across trial conditions.

s.defn: To exhaust or deplete a resource through use; to consume the available amount.
ex: The team used up the remaining budget.
Over the course of the experiment, resources were gradually used and depleted.

s.defn: Past habitual action or state expressed with the periphrastic construction used to, indicating that something was true in the past but is no longer the case.
ex: In historical linguistics, researchers used to analyze corpora of older texts.
The phrase used to signals past habitual actions in English.

s.defn: Employed or utilized for a particular purpose in scholarly discourse; applied to a task or object.
ex: The term is used to denote a controlled experimental condition.
This variable is used to indicate treatment status.

s.defn: Secondhand or previously owned; not new.
ex: A used car may require inspection before sale.
Used equipment should be certified for reliability.

s.defn: Accustomed to; familiar with due to repeated exposure; not new.
ex: Researchers became used to the noise after acclimation.
Participants were used to the testing environment following a practice trial.

s.defn: Worn or consumed; no longer in pristine condition due to prior use.
ex: Used equipment exhibited visible wear and reduced efficiency.
Old but used components showed signs of fatigue.

s.defn: Neat and orderly; arranged in a structured, tidy physical arrangement.
ex: The organized desk helps students locate materials quickly.
Organized folders on the desk save time during tests.

s.defn: Having plans and resources arranged in advance; prepared to act and learn.
ex: The organized study plan helps students finish lessons.
A teacher uses an organized calendar to schedule activities.

s.defn: Thinking or approaching tasks in a systematic, methodical way.
ex: She keeps organized notes to track experiments.
Organized data allow clearer comparisons across trials.

s.defn: To arrange or plan in a methodical, orderly way.
ex: The class organized the science fair timetable.
The librarian organized the library by subject.

s.defn: Having been arranged into an orderly form.
ex: The files were organized by date.
The event was organized into five workshops.

s.defn: A measured piece of ground owned or used by people in past communities.
ex: Early settlers received a farm plot near the river for crops.
The town map shows each family's plot and its boundaries.

s.defn: A secret plan by a group to change government power or carry out a political action in the past.
ex: Historians studied the assassination plot against the ruler.
School sources explain how a secret plot started the rebellion.

s.defn: To secretly plan or arrange a coordinated action against a person or government in a historical context.
ex: Historians study how groups plot to change a monarchy.
The class read about people who plotted against a king.

s.defn: To mark places or events on a map or timeline to show where or when things happened.
ex: Students plot battle sites on a classroom map to study campaigns.
We plotted each event on the timeline to show order.

s.defn: To draw or place data points on a graph to show patterns in historical records over time.
ex: They plotted population numbers to show growth after the war.
Students plotted rainfall data for a historical climate study.

s.defn: A noun for a substance from which water or other diluting agents have been removed, resulting in a thick, concentrated form used in recipes or further processing.
ex: Orange concentrate is mixed with water to make juice.
Tomato concentrate thickens sauces with a rich, savory flavor.

s.defn: To direct one's attention and mental effort toward a task or objective.
ex: During the tests, students concentrate on solving each problem.
The teacher asked the class to concentrate on reading the passage.

s.defn: To make a liquid more concentrated by removing solvent.
ex: Researchers concentrated the sample by heating the beaker.
Juice can be concentrated by evaporating water from it.

s.defn: To bring people or things together into a common location.
ex: The crowd concentrated near the stage for the science fair.
Students concentrated the team in the gym for the activity.

s.defn: Anatomical region of the upper trunk comprising the thorax and rib cage, between the neck and the abdomen, that encloses the heart and lungs.
ex: The chest cavity houses the heart and lungs.
In radiology, a chest radiograph assesses cardiopulmonary structures.

s.defn: A large strong box with a hinged lid used for storage, typically made of wood.
ex: The wooden chest contained rare manuscripts.
A toy chest stood at the foot of the bed.

s.defn: To receive and control a moving ball or object by allowing it to contact the chest, typically in ball sports, in order to reduce velocity and enable subsequent action such as a pass or dribble.
ex: The forward chested the pass to maintain possession under pressure.
During drills, players chested the ball to control it before passing.

s.defn: To provide instruction and experiences that develop a student’s knowledge and skills.
ex: Parents educate children by reading together daily.
Teachers educate students through guided practice and feedback.

s.defn: To cultivate understanding and values by guiding thinking through discussion and example.
ex: Educators aim to educate students about fairness and responsibility.
Parents educate children by discussing choices and consequences.

s.defn: A strong feeling of enthusiasm, interest, or eagerness about a topic or activity.
ex: The lab activity sparked excitement about science.
Students showed excitement when solving challenging problems.

s.defn: A temporary emotional arousal in response to a stimulating event such as a science demo or new discovery.
ex: A quick demo created a buzz of excitement.
The surprise experiment increased students' excitement.

s.defn: A contagious feeling of enthusiasm shared among people in a group.
ex: Excitement spread through the class after the announcement.
The auditorium buzzed with growing excitement before the performance.

s.defn: A person who has been rejected by a group or society as undesirable or unfit.
ex: A new student was treated as a reject by the club.
The social reject felt left out at lunch.

s.defn: An item that has been rejected during quality control because it does not meet required standards.
ex: The bolt is a reject because it is bent.
Factory rejects go into the scrap bin.

s.defn: A collection or pile of items that have been rejected, often kept separate from good items.
ex: Rejects are stored in the reject pile.
Items in the reject bin wait for disposal.

s.defn: To refuse to accept or approve something such as an offer, proposal, or request.
ex: The school board rejected the field trip proposal after reviewing safety plans.
Students should not reject constructive feedback without considering the evidence.

s.defn: To deny a claim as true or valid; to declare it false or unsupported by evidence.
ex: The editor rejected the claim as unsupported by data.
The teacher rejected the hypothesis because the data did not support it.

s.defn: To refuse to allow someone to join or participate; to deny entry or membership.
ex: The club rejected his application for membership.
The team rejected several applicants during tryouts.

s.defn: A written or told account that records historical events in order and explains what happened.
ex: The class read a historical narrative about the settlement of the town.
Students compared two narratives to find differences in facts.

s.defn: An organizing explanation that connects events and causes to help people understand the past.
ex: A historian's narrative can explain causes and effects clearly.
We discussed how different narratives shape what we remember.

s.defn: A first person account that tells personal experiences or family history in a historical context.
ex: She wrote a personal narrative about her grandparents' immigration.
His firsthand account helped classmates understand daily life long ago.

s.defn: Relating to or forming a storylike account of events used to explain historical people or places to learners.
ex: The lesson used a narrative timeline to show how the town grew over years.
Students wrote a narrative paragraph describing the explorer's route and actions.

s.defn: Describing language or evidence that recounts events in order rather than analyzing causes or arguments.
ex: Teachers asked learners to mark narrative evidence separate from cause explanations.
A narrative report lists events in order without deep analysis of why they happened.

s.defn: A toxic substance that can cause illness or death if eaten, breathed, or absorbed through the skin.
ex: Arsenic is a well known poison used in history.
Cyanide is a fast acting poison that can be deadly.

s.defn: A nonliteral use of poison to describe something that harms or corrupts people, relationships, or processes.
ex: Gossip can act as social poison, damaging trust.
Prejudice is a poison that weakens communities.

s.defn: To administer a toxic substance to cause harm or death.
ex: Exposure to certain heavy metals can poison the bloodstream if not treated promptly.
A toxin can poison cells by interfering with respiration or metabolism.

s.defn: To contaminate a substance or environment with poison or toxins.
ex: Spilling pesticide can poison the water supply and threaten local ecosystems.
Improper preparation may poison people who eat the food.

s.defn: To ruin or corrupt something by spreading harmful information or biased content (often used idiomatically as well).
ex: Spreading rumors can poison the well of classmates opinions about a project.
Biased reports may poison the audience's trust in science data.

s.defn: The top or lid that closes a container such as a pot or jar.
ex: The pot lid fits snugly to keep moisture inside.
Always place the lid on the jar to prevent spills.

s.defn: A protective or decorative outer layer that covers a surface.
ex: The table received a protective cover to prevent stains.
The book has a durable fabric cover.

s.defn: An insurance policy or amount of protection against risk provided by an insurer.
ex: The policy provides medical cover.
Home cover helps pay for repairs after a storm.

s.defn: To place something over or on top of another object, forming a layer for protection, concealment, or insulation.
ex: The lid covers the pot to keep heat inside.
A glaze was used to cover the ceramic surface.

s.defn: To deal with, discuss, or include within a book, lesson, or conversation.
ex: The chapter covers the causes of the Civil War.
The lesson covers fractions as part of the unit.

s.defn: To provide protection or payment under a policy; to insure or reimburse costs.
ex: The policy covers medical expenses.
The warranty will cover parts for one year.

s.defn: To happen or take place at a particular time or place.
ex: The festival occurs each summer in the town square.
Lightning occurs during storms.

s.defn: To come into someone's mind; to be thought of.
ex: A question occurred to her while reading the page.
It occurred to him to check the data after the lesson.

s.defn: To carry out a careful, systematic inquiry to discover facts about something.
ex: In science, students investigate how plants respond to light levels.
A teacher asks students to investigate a simple mystery in their project.

s.defn: To inspect or examine something to verify facts, assess safety, or determine correctness or quality.
ex: The safety team will investigate the reported hazard.
A student will investigate why the data shows an unexpected result.

s.defn: To study a question for a school project by gathering sources and evidence and drawing conclusions.
ex: For the science fair, students investigate the best material for insulating a cup.
They will investigate how plants grow under different colors of light.

s.defn: The physical force that causes objects to move toward each other, such as gravity or magnetism.
ex: Gravity provides the attraction that keeps objects in orbit.
A magnet pulls iron toward its surface.

s.defn: The quality that attracts interest or admiration; the appeal or charm of something.
ex: The science project has strong appeal for students.
Clear explanations increase student attraction to the topic.

s.defn: A place that draws visitors due to its significance or appeal.
ex: The Louvre is a famous tourist attraction.
National parks are popular tourist attractions.

s.defn: A fossil fuel consisting of carbon-rich sedimentary rock formed from plant material, used primarily for energy production.
ex: Coal remains a major energy source for electricity generation worldwide.
Industrial plants historically relied on coal to heat steam boilers.

s.defn: A lump or piece of coal, especially a discrete unit used as a fuel.
ex: A single coal lump was placed on the fire.
Workers loaded a lump of coal into the furnace.

s.defn: To load or supply a furnace, engine, or other apparatus with coal as fuel, thereby providing energy for combustion.
ex: The locomotive was coaled before departure.
Crew members coaled the boiler to restore heat output.

s.defn: The people of a country or community regarded as a group; ordinary people.
ex: The folk in the village participated in the project.
Researchers interviewed the folk about daily routines.

s.defn: A group of people sharing a distinct culture within a region.
ex: The folk of Scotland celebrate with bagpipes.
The local folk preserve language and customs.

s.defn: Stories, legends, or songs handed down within a culture.
ex: Students studied folktales from the region.
They performed folk songs during the cultural presentation.

s.defn: Adjective sense 1: Of or relating to ordinary people or everyday life; not specialized or elite.
ex: The teacher explains folk wisdom about saving for emergencies.
Students compare folk tales to everyday life in history.

s.defn: Adjective sense 2: Relating to traditional culture and customs of a people; used for arts and practices handed down through generations.
ex: The museum displays folk crafts from rural regions.
Educators discuss folk songs in regional history units.

s.defn: Having high value due to usefulness or monetary worth.
ex: This tool is valuable because it saves time in experiments.
A valuable resource like this book helps students finish assignments.

s.defn: Having emotional significance; valued as a cherished or treasured object or relationship.
ex: The bracelet is valuable to me as a family heirloom.
Old letters are valuable keepsakes that teach family history.

s.defn: Having monetary worth; capable of being bought or sold for money.
ex: Gold and silver are valuable metals used in jewelry.
A valuable asset can increase a company's market value.

s.defn: A valuable is an object that is worth a lot of money or holds significant sentimental value.
ex: The ancient coin is a valuable because of its historical significance.
In class, students catalog valuables to learn about cultural value.

s.defn: Of or relating to the east; located toward the east or in the eastern part of something.
ex: The eastern coastline experiences higher rainfall.
Eastern Europe has undergone significant political changes.

s.defn: Predominantly; chiefly; used to indicate that something constitutes the greatest part or extent of a situation or statement.
ex: The population mainly consists of young adults.
The report mainly analyzes long-term outcomes.

s.defn: As a sentence adverb or discourse marker, mainly is used to indicate focus on the principal aspect of a proposition or to constrain the scope of a claim within discourse.
ex: The study mainly focuses on data analysis.
Mainly, the findings support the proposed model.

s.defn: A formal prohibition issued by an authority that forbids a specific action or item.
ex: The school issued a ban on cell phone use during class.
The new travel ban restricted entry for several countries.

s.defn: The state of something being prohibited or the act of prohibiting.
ex: A campus policy created a ban on single use plastics.
The decree established the ban on certain items.

s.defn: To officially prohibit an activity, item, or practice by rules, laws, or authority.
ex: The school bans cell phones during class to reduce interruptions.
The city bans smoking in indoor workplaces.

s.defn: To exclude a person or thing from participation in a group, event, or location.
ex: The coach banned the player from the game for cheating.
The club banned her from the meeting due to misconduct.

s.defn: To prohibit something temporarily or under a specific condition or policy.
ex: During exams the school bans phone use for the week.
A temporary ban is imposed on certain apps.

s.defn: A group of buildings or facilities that are connected or located close together and treated as one unit.
ex: The apartment complex has a courtyard and many apartments.
The school complex includes classrooms, a gym, and a library.

s.defn: A pattern of related emotions and ideas that can influence a person's thoughts or behavior.
ex: He has a money complex that makes him reluctant to spend.
A teacher described the mother complex in simple language.

s.defn: A group or collection of related issues or tasks that are connected and can be difficult to understand or solve.
ex: The science project covers a complex of topics.
The homework includes a problem complex with several tasks.

s.defn: Not easily understood or explained because it consists of many parts that are connected.
ex: The science experiment had a complex setup that confused beginners.
A complex math problem requires several strategies to solve.

s.defn: The process by which a living thing or a learner grows, matures, and becomes more capable.
ex: Researchers study childhood development to learn how people learn.
A student's reading development shows steady progress this semester.

s.defn: The plan or sequence of actions designed to create or improve something.
ex: The curriculum development team revised the math module.
We evaluated the development plan before starting the project.

s.defn: An event or change in a situation or story that affects outcomes.
ex: The plot twist changed how the characters solved the problem.
A new incident shifted the class project plan.

s.defn: The right or ability to use or enter something such as a place or service.
ex: Students gain access to the science lab after safety training.
Library cards provide access to online databases.

s.defn: A way or means of entering a place or approaching something.
ex: The doorway provides access to the gym.
The library uses a secure gateway for student login.

s.defn: The act of obtaining or retrieving data from a computer or database.
ex: Students must sign in to gain data access.
The librarian grants access to the archive database.

s.defn: To gain entry or passage to a place or area.
ex: Students can access the library after presenting ID.
A password allows users to access the network.

s.defn: To obtain or view information stored in a computer system or database.
ex: Students can access course materials through the online portal.
The database lets teachers access records securely.

s.defn: To have the right or possibility to use or benefit from a resource or service.
ex: Students have access to the school library during study periods.
Public access to the museum is available on weekends.

s.defn: Not direct; taking a route or method that avoids a straight path or immediate connection.
ex: The indirect route to the science fair added extra travel time.
Teachers use indirect methods in problem solving to encourage inference.

s.defn: In language or communication, implied or not stated explicitly; hinted at rather than declared.
ex: The author used indirect language to suggest a theme without naming it directly.
The feedback was indirect, pointing to improvements without listing them all.

s.defn: In reasoning or measurement, leading to a result through intermediate steps rather than a direct assertion.
ex: In geometry, an indirect proof shows the result by assuming the opposite and deriving a contradiction.
A common indirect method of estimation uses related data to infer the value.

s.defn: The act or process of producing printed matter by applying ink to a surface through a printing press or other device, including the use of digital printers.
ex: The printing process can be optimized through digital workflows.
Digital printing enables rapid job turnaround and customization.

s.defn: The industry or business involved in the production of printed materials such as books, newspapers, packaging, and promotional materials.
ex: The printing industry has consolidated many mid sized shops.
Automation and outsourcing affect commercial printing markets.

s.defn: A single printed copy or impression produced by a printing process; an individual impression of an image or text.
ex: A single printing bears the artist's watermark.
The edition is limited to twenty five printings.

s.defn: To reproduce text or images on paper or other substrates by applying ink through a printing press or digital printer.
ex: Scholarly manuscripts require high volume printing for multiple copies.
Academic publishers rely on precise printing for reproducible figures.

s.defn: To output textual data to a display device such as a monitor or terminal.
ex: The script prints the value to the console.
Debug messages are often sent as text output.

s.defn: Relating to the process of producing printed matter by mechanical reproduction.
ex: The study analyzes the printing costs across different vendor contracts.
Advances in printing technology have reduced turnaround times.

s.defn: Describing output or materials prepared for immediate reproduction by printing equipment.
ex: Submit a print-ready manuscript to the publisher.
A reproduction-ready file must pass the preflight check.

s.defn: The layer of gases that surrounds Earth or another planet.
ex: Earth's atmosphere contains mostly nitrogen and oxygen.
The atmosphere becomes thinner at higher altitudes.

s.defn: The mood or feeling created by a place or setting.
ex: The classroom atmosphere can affect how much students learn.
A friendly atmosphere helps readers relax while studying.

s.defn: The overall impression or tone of a situation, work, or event.
ex: The novel's atmosphere supports its suspense and mystery.
The school bulletin creates a welcoming atmosphere for students.

s.defn: The act of identifying similarities and differences between historical people events or sources to understand causes and effects.
ex: Students made a comparison of two explorers to find different causes.
The teacher asked for a comparison of primary and secondary sources.

s.defn: A structured tool such as a chart or diagram that organizes similarities and differences for classroom study.
ex: She filled a comparison chart to show differences between colonial settlements.
Use a Venn diagram for a clear comparison of events.

s.defn: A measurement or description that shows how numbers dates or amounts differ between historical items.
ex: The census comparison showed population growth between 1800 and 1850.
Comparing dates clarified the order of related events across regions.

s.defn: In educational contexts, practical means useful or usable in real world tasks and experiments rather than in theory alone.
ex: Students design a practical science project using household materials.
A practical reading plan helps with daily routines.

s.defn: Relating to action rather than theory and emphasizing what can be done in real settings.
ex: The teacher selects a pragmatic activity for the class.
A feasible plan fits the available time and materials.

s.defn: Relating to everyday efficiency and safety, choosing actions that are economical and prudent.
ex: A practical safety check prevents accidents in the lab.
Choose a practical method that fits the science project timeline.

s.defn: Legally found to have committed an offense; having criminal liability.
ex: The court found the defendant guilty beyond reasonable doubt.
A guilty verdict establishes legal liability in criminal procedure.

s.defn: Experiencing guilt or moral responsibility for a wrongdoing.
ex: He felt guilty after the ethical lapse in judgment.
A guilty conscience can influence decision making in research ethics.

s.defn: The noun guilty denotes a person who has been found legally or morally culpable for a crime or offense; the offender or wrongdoer.
ex: The guilty were subject to restitution and sanctions.
Jurors determined the guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

s.defn: A collective noun referring to the set of individuals who have been determined to be guilty in a particular case or context; the group of offenders contextual to a given inquiry or jurisdiction.
ex: In the trial, the guilty were detained for further proceedings.
Criminology distinguishes the guilty from the innocent in case studies.

s.defn: A collection of items chosen as a unit.
ex: We arranged a tea set on the dining table.
A set of flashcards helps practice math facts.

s.defn: A well defined collection of objects or numbers that share a property.
ex: The set of even numbers is infinite.
An empty set contains no elements.

s.defn: The scenery and props arranged on a stage.
ex: The stage set included a painted backdrop and desks.
We studied how changing the set affects mood in a scene.

s.defn: A portion of a match consisting of games.
ex: She won the first set 6 games to 3.
The final set decided the match in tennis.

s.defn: To put or place something in a fixed position.
ex: The librarian set the books on the shelf.
Students should set their pencils on the desk before the bell.

s.defn: To establish or decide something such as rules, dates, or goals.
ex: The class set a due date for the assignment.
The teacher set goals for the semester.

s.defn: To become firm or solid as a result of cooling or drying.
ex: The jelly will set in the fridge.
The cement will set as it dries.

s.defn: To adjust something to a desired level or setting.
ex: She set the volume to a safe level.
We set the thermostat to a comfortable temperature.

s.defn: Fixed or predetermined; not subject to change.
ex: A set date for the field trip helps organizers plan classroom activities.
The price is set at 50 dollars and will not increase this quarter.

s.defn: Ready for immediate use or action; prepared beforehand.
ex: The set temperature was recorded before the science experiment began.
Make sure the set timer is started before the lesson proceeds.

s.defn: A small rounded piece of bread baked as part of a meal.
ex: The soup was served with a warm roll.
We split a buttered roll after the lesson.

s.defn: A list of people or things, used to record attendance or to call out names.
ex: The teacher checked the roll to see who was present.
Students lined up as the roll was called.

s.defn: A rolled length of film or tape wound into a cylinder.
ex: The photographer loaded a fresh film roll into the camera.
The editor rewound the film roll after filming.

s.defn: To move along a surface by turning over and around, as a wheel or ball does.
ex: The ball rolls across the gym floor.
A wagon rolls smoothly downhill.

s.defn: To travel or move by rolling on wheels; to move from one place to another in a vehicle.
ex: The cart rolled down the hill.
The bus rolled along the street.

s.defn: To flatten or shape dough or other soft material by pressing and rolling with a rolling pin.
ex: Roll the dough until smooth.
Roll out the pastry for cookies.

s.defn: The act of carrying out or doing something, especially how well a task is done.
ex: The student's performance on the science task improved after practice.
A teacher rates performance by how carefully steps are completed.

s.defn: A public display of skill or talent done for an audience such as a concert, recital, or play.
ex: The school chorus gave a lively performance.
The class talent show will be a short public performance.

s.defn: The manner in which a device or system operates or functions, especially how fast or efficiently it runs.
ex: The computer's performance improved after the upgrade.
We measure device performance using speed and reliability tests.

s.defn: Mood as a noun is a temporary state of mind or feeling that can influence how a person perceives information and behaves.
ex: Her mood changed after receiving the good news.
A teacher may consider mood when asking students to explain their reasoning.

s.defn: Mood in grammar is a grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the action, such as stating facts, issuing commands, or expressing wishes.
ex: The indicative mood states facts.
The imperative mood gives commands to do something.

s.defn: To indicate or describe the connection between two or more things.
ex: The diagram relates the cause to the effect.
Students relate data from experiments to the hypothesis.

s.defn: To recount or narrate a story or event in a sequence.
ex: The elder related the case study in sequence.
She related an anecdote to illustrate the point.

s.defn: To bear on or be connected to a topic or issue; to pertain.
ex: These findings relate to the main question.
The evidence relates to classroom practice.

s.defn: The muscular organ on the floor of the mouth used for tasting, swallowing, and articulating speech.
ex: Doctors examine the tongue to assess taste and swallowing.
A healthy tongue helps articulate sounds in speech therapy.

s.defn: A language spoken by a community; the native language of a person.
ex: Her mother tongue is English, learned at home.
Students study how many languages exist in the world.

s.defn: A projecting piece that fits into another part, as the tongue of a shoe or buckle.
ex: The shoe tongue cushions the top of the foot.
The belt buckle tongue slides through the strap holes.

s.defn: To touch or lick with the tongue, especially to taste, clean, or explore a surface.
ex: The cat tongued the milk from the saucer.
She tongued the frosting from her finger.

s.defn: The final part of a story, experiment, or discussion where the end is explained.
ex: The conclusion of the story revealed the hero's fate.
The scientist described the conclusion of the experiment and what it means.

s.defn: The act of forming a conclusion from evidence; the reasoning process used to decide something after looking at information.
ex: From the data the researchers drew a conclusion about the cause.
Her conclusion came after comparing several sources.

s.defn: The final summary of the main points in a piece of writing or speech.
ex: The conclusion of the essay restates the main idea.
In the conclusion, the author highlights the key takeaways.

s.defn: To cease active employment or service, usually because of age or long tenure.
ex: The professor retired after forty years of service.
Military personnel retire after twenty years of duty.

s.defn: To withdraw from participation in a competition or activity.

ex: The team winged the data collection protocol.
Researchers often wing the presentation when data are incomplete.

s.defn: To pass quickly; to move forward swiftly, as time is perceived to be propelled.
ex: The hour wings by during late night data analysis.
Days can wing by when distractions are few in the lab.

s.defn: Not smooth; having an uneven surface or edge.
ex: The wood has a rough surface with a bumpy feel.
Sandpaper created a rough texture on the board.

s.defn: Not exact; approximate or rough in calculation or measurement.
ex: The teacher gave a rough estimate of the project time.
They used a rough calculation to plan the lesson.

s.defn: Harsh or crude in manner or treatment; not gentle.
ex: The coach spoke in a rough voice during practice.
Rough handling damaged the science equipment.

s.defn: The quality of being uneven or coarse in texture or surface; the characteristic of a surface that feels rough or jagged.
ex: The rough surface of the sandpaper shows a coarse texture.
Students compare rough and smooth materials to study texture in a science lesson.

s.defn: The state of having paid work; the condition of being employed.
ex: Many students seek employment after completing a course.
A summer job provides real world employment experience.

s.defn: The act of employing or using something to accomplish a task.
ex: The employment of new technology improves classroom efficiency.
Efficient scheduling increases the employment of available resources.

s.defn: Opportunities for work available within a community or industry.
ex: The city promotes youth employment through summer programs.
Many families look for employment opportunities near home.

s.defn: To cause mild displeasure or bother in someone by provoking a reaction that is not intense; to irritate without strong hostility.
ex: The constant interruptions annoy researchers during data collection.
Frequent delays annoy students awaiting feedback on drafts.

s.defn: To harass or vex someone by repeating actions, to create persistent nuisance or disruption.
ex: The sales representative's persistent calls annoyed customers.
Repeated scrutiny by the committee annoyed the editor.

s.defn: Feeling or showing slight anger or irritation in response to a perceived inconvenience or provocation.
ex: Participants reported annoyed responses to procedural delays.
The committee noted an annoyed reaction to the revised protocol.

s.defn: The aesthetic property of an object that gives rise to pleasure or admiration, typically through harmony of form, proportion, and color, in nature, art, or discourse.
ex: The symmetry and proportion contribute to the beauty of the sculpture.
Scholars analyze beauty as an objective or cultural construct.

s.defn: A person who is aesthetically attractive; an individual regarded as a beauty.
ex: She was widely regarded as a beauty in her school.
The beauty captivated the audience with poise on stage.

s.defn: An interjective expression used to convey enthusiastic approval or satisfaction with a result or performance.
ex: The data align with the hypothesis Beauty!
The result meets the criteria Beauty!

s.defn: An interjective expression of aesthetic admiration for beauty in nature or art.
ex: The sunset confirmed the observer's sense of Beauty!
The sculpture expresses harmony and Beauty!

s.defn: An interjection used to mark a neat or elegant solution or idea in formal reasoning or discourse.
ex: A neat trick in the derivation Beauty!
The final step reveals a clever solution Beauty!

s.defn: To say something again or perform an action again, often for emphasis, clarification, or accuracy.
ex: The researcher repeated the measurement to verify accuracy.
Participants repeated the question to confirm understanding.

s.defn: To occur again; to recur.
ex: The symptoms recurred after the initial improvement.
A second outbreak recurred during the study period.

s.defn: Happening again or occurring more than once in a given context.
ex: Repeated measurements were taken to reduce sampling error.
The data set included repeated observations across sessions.

s.defn: Relating to the act or pattern of repeating in a methodological or cognitive context.
ex: The study utilized repeated measures to monitor within subject variability.
Repeated exposure to stimuli can strengthen associative learning.

s.defn: Relating to the use or effect of repeating words or ideas for emphasis in discourse.
ex: The author employs repeated motifs for rhetorical emphasis.
A repeated refrain appears across chapters to underscore central themes.

s.defn: In physics and chemistry, relating to the nucleus of an atom; used to describe processes such as fission, fusion, and radioactive decay.
ex: Nuclear fission releases energy when heavy nuclei split.
Nuclear models describe interactions within the atomic nucleus.

s.defn: Relating to the nucleus of a cell; pertaining to cellular nucleus and its components.
ex: The nuclear envelope encloses the nucleus.
Nuclear pores regulate traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm.

s.defn: Relating to weapons or energy produced by nuclear reactions; in contexts such as weapons development and power generation.
ex: Nuclear weapons pose serious strategic risks.
Nuclear power plants generate electricity.

s.defn: Relating to the central or core part of a system or structure; used metaphorically to denote central importance.
ex: The nuclear family includes parents and dependent children.
A small team served as the nuclear core of the project.

s.defn: The capacity to exert physical force or perform work with the body.
ex: The student demonstrated physical strength during the gym assessment.
Strength is measured by how much load a material can bear.

s.defn: A person’s moral or emotional resilience; robustness of character.
ex: Her moral strength helped her resist peer pressure.
Character strength grows through steady practice and reflection.

s.defn: The magnitude or level of a quantity such as wind, light, or a signal.
ex: The wind strength prevented sailing in the afternoon.
We tested the signal strength to ensure reception.

s.defn: Causing mild irritation or nuisance, typically used in academic evaluation to denote a factor that provokes annoyance without severe disruption.
ex: The annoying artifact introduced bias into the results.
Participants cited an annoying interruption that distracted focus.

s.defn: Describing phenomena, behaviors, or conditions that persistently irritate or disrupt processes, thereby hindering attention or efficiency in academic or professional contexts.
ex: A persistent noise was a vexing problem in the lab schedule.
The study noted annoying delays in data collection.

s.defn: To irritate or bother someone through ongoing actions or remarks, often by persistently interfering with their activities or comfort.
ex: The constant interruptions are annoying the researchers.
Ambient noise is annoying to participants in the study.

s.defn: The present participle form of annoy used as an adjective to describe something that causes irritation or nuisance.
ex: The constant interruptions are annoying to staff.
Annoying delays disrupted the data collection schedule.

s.defn: Not clear or easy to understand; feeling bewildered or puzzled.
ex: Students looked confused after the science demonstration.
The directions were unclear, leaving the class confused.

s.defn: Not orderly or well organized; mixed up or disordered.
ex: The worksheet layout was confused and hard to follow.
The filing system was disorganized and hard to use.

s.defn: To cause someone to be perplexed or uncertain by presenting unclear or conflicting information.
ex: The teacher's overly complex directions confused several students during the science review.
A noisy chart could confuse readers about the steps required.

s.defn: To confuse two or more things with one another or to mistake one thing for another.
ex: Students may confuse the terms hypothesis and theory during early lessons.
If you mix up the measurements, you might confuse the outcomes.

s.defn: To become perplexed or bewildered; to feel unclear about something.
ex: I was confused by the new algebra notation after the lesson.
The diagram remained confusing until the teacher explained the legend.

s.defn: Not occurring often; scarce in number or frequency.
ex: Rare fossils were found in the quarry.
A rare bird was spotted near the marsh.

s.defn: Extremely unusual or noteworthy in quality or occurrence.
ex: Her rare talent impressed the panel.
The discovery was a rare scientific breakthrough.

s.defn: Not fully cooked; cooked to a low degree.
ex: Serving rare steak can be unsafe if not cooked properly.
The waiter recommended rare steak for flavor.

s.defn: In fashion; current and stylish in appearance.
ex: The runway show featured fashionable outfits that impressed shoppers.
Our school project requires fashionable presentation and clear attire.

s.defn: Describing dress or behavior that conforms to accepted standards in a specific group or setting.
ex: In school clubs, appropriate outfits still look fashionable.
A fashionable color may be appropriate for a science fair.

s.defn: The obligation to carry out duties or take care of someone or something.
ex: Students show responsibility by turning in homework on time.
Parents have responsibility for guiding younger siblings.

s.defn: The personal quality of being reliable and trustworthy in fulfilling duties.
ex: A person with responsibility follows through on commitments.
Responsibility includes being honest when plans change.

s.defn: A specific duty or task assigned to a person.
ex: Your science project is your responsibility.
Each student has responsibility to finish the book report.

s.defn: A male religious leader authorized to perform sacred rites in a Christian church.
ex: The parish priest administered the baptism.
A priest leads the congregation during the Sunday liturgy.

s.defn: The body of ordained priests forming the clergy of a religious tradition; the priesthood.
ex: He joined the priesthood after seminary.
In Catholicism the priesthood carries sacramental responsibilities.

s.defn: A person who plans and coordinates events or activities.
ex: The student club appointed an organizer to coordinate the fundraiser.
A good organizer helps teams meet deadlines.

s.defn: A device or container used to hold and sort items.
ex: The desk organizer keeps pencils sorted on the desk.
A file organizer helps students manage worksheets.

s.defn: A visual tool that helps students organize information.
ex: The teacher uses a graphic organizer to plan the essay.
A mind map helps students arrange ideas visually.

s.defn: In meteorology, a hurricane is a tropical cyclone in the Atlantic or northeastern Pacific with sustained winds of at least 74 mph (119 km/h) and a well defined circulation.
ex: Forecasting hurricane tracks requires satellite data and atmospheric measurements.
Coastal risk assessments incorporate historical hurricane frequency and intensity data.

s.defn: A metaphorical use of hurricane to denote a person or event that is violently disruptive or overwhelming.
ex: The policy proposal faced a hurricane of criticism from scientists.
A hurricane of protests swept through the campuses.

s.defn: A portrait is a painting, drawing, photograph, or sculpture that represents a person, especially the face.
ex: The portrait of the founder hangs in the school library.
Learners study portraits to observe facial features and proportion.

s.defn: A portrait can also mean a person’s public image or representation formed by others, often described in media or biography.
ex: The article offered a portrait of the scientist as careful and ethical.
The biography presents a portrait of the author during early career.

s.defn: In literature, a portrait is a vivid description or portrayal of a person or character.
ex: The memoir offers a warm portrait of family life.
The author provides a stark portrait of hardship.

s.defn: Having a strong belief in oneself or one's abilities; not doubting one's capacity.
ex: The student is confident about the upcoming test.
Her confident demeanor impressed the panel.

s.defn: Having good grounds to believe something; supported by evidence or reasoning.
ex: The researchers are confident that the results support the hypothesis.
Educators feel confident about the plan given robust evidence.

s.defn: In demeanor or appearance, showing calm assurance and poise.
ex: She spoke with a confident and composed tone.
He entered the room with a confident poised posture.

s.defn: A garment worn on the hand to protect against injury, contamination, or cold.
ex: In the laboratory, researchers wore sterile gloves during procedures to prevent contamination.
Cold-weather workers rely on gloves to maintain dexterity while exposed to low temperatures.

s.defn: A specialized form of handwear designed for particular activities, often padded for impact and grip.
ex: Baseball gloves cushion impacts and facilitate catching.
Boxing gloves provide padded protection while allowing controlled punching.

s.defn: To put on gloves; to cover the hands with gloves.
ex: The technician gloved the hands before handling hazardous samples.
The surgeon gloved the patient prior to incision.

s.defn: To catch or handle with a glove; to catch a ball using a glove.
ex: The fielder gloved the ball in the seventh inning.
She gloved the ball cleanly off the hop.

s.defn: To enclose or shield with a glove like covering for protection.
ex: The reactor vessel was gloved in a thick lead shield.
The sterile chamber was gloved in a polymer coating to prevent contamination.

s.defn: Horror in general refers to an intense fear, dread, or aversion experienced in response to threat, danger, or morally disturbing stimuli.
ex: Participants reported heightened horror when exposed to graphic violence.
Horror responses in literature are often linked to suspenseful threat.

s.defn: A genre of fiction or film designed to evoke fear, dread, or disgust through suspense, the supernatural, or morbid imagery.
ex: Horror cinema often relies on suspenseful pacing and sound design.
Horror fiction frequently explores mortality and transgression.

s.defn: A moral or visceral reaction of revulsion or nausea to acts or scenes perceived as morally reprehensible.
ex: Moral horror emerges when fiction depicts egregious acts.
Scholars analyze horror as a response to ethical transgression.

s.defn: Having accountability for actions or outcomes; being answerable for fulfilling duties in legal, ethical, or institutional contexts.
ex: The principal is responsible for compliance with the policy.
Researchers are responsible for obtaining informed consent and ethics approval.

s.defn: Capable of being trusted to perform tasks carefully and reliably; dependable.
ex: A responsible researcher ensures data integrity.
Students are expected to be responsible in class and labs.

s.defn: Describing actions or policies that carefully consider ethical norms and social consequences and aim to minimize harm; conducted with prudent and ethical regard for broader impacts.
ex: Responsible budgeting helps prevent deficits in the organization.
Environmental and social outcomes depend on responsible resource management.

s.defn: An emotional state characterized by sadness or displeasure caused by unmet expectations or hopes.
ex: The student was disappointed after the exam results were released.
Researchers were disappointed by the initial findings despite robust methodology.

s.defn: An evaluative descriptor applied to outcomes performances or results that fail to meet expectations, provoking disappointment.
ex: The committee was disappointed with the replication results.
The turnout was disappointing to the organizers.

s.defn: To cause to feel disappointment by failing to meet expectations; to fail to fulfill anticipated outcomes for a recipient.
ex: The study results disappointed the committee.
The policy changes disappointed the stakeholders.

s.defn: To experience disappointment; to feel unhappy because something did not meet expectations.
ex: Investors were disappointed by the results.
Scholars were disappointed with the null findings.

s.defn: In a manner that occurs at regular intervals or follows a predictable pattern.
ex: Students should review notes regularly to retain information.
The timer rang regularly every ten minutes during the experiment.

s.defn: In a habitual way, as part of a routine or standard practice.
ex: She regularly participates in science clubs after school.
We regularly check in with the mentor during projects.

s.defn: In a way that is standard or typical, following normal procedures or expectations.
ex: The method is regularly used in grade level experiments.
All students should record results in a regularly structured format.

s.defn: A formal observance or ceremony to honor a person, event, or achievement.
ex: The award ceremony marked a formal celebration of student achievement.
A campus observance honored the milestone with invited guests.

s.defn: A festive or joyful social event, such as a party, held to honor or enjoy a particular occasion.
ex: Students planned a school celebration to mark the end of the unit.
Cultural celebrations often involve music, food, and shared stories.

s.defn: The act or process of celebrating; the expression of joy or admiration.
ex: The act of celebration strengthens community bonds.
People express celebration through music, dance, and shared meals.

s.defn: In pieces; separated into parts; not connected.
ex: The mosaic shattered and lay apart in fragments.
The mechanism came apart under stress.

s.defn: At a spatial distance; not near or contiguous.
ex: The houses stood apart along the street.
Distances apart persisted across the valley.

s.defn: Excluding or excepting; with the exception of.
ex: Apart from the cost, the plan was viable.
Apart from a few glitches, the system works.

s.defn: Of or relating to objects that are physically separated, existing at a distance from one another; not in contact.
ex: The components lay apart on the bench to prevent interference.
The probes were placed apart to avoid thermal coupling.

s.defn: Designated or reserved for a particular use or purpose; kept aside from general use.
ex: The emergency funds were kept apart from everyday finances.
The funds are kept apart for future research.

s.defn: Used with from to indicate an exception or exclusion; denotes that a specified item is not included in a statement or set.
ex: Apart from minor deviations, the results corroborate the hypothesis.
The method yielded reliable data apart from a single outlier.

s.defn: Not movable; firmly attached to a surface so it cannot be moved.
ex: The shelf is fixed to the wall with brackets.
The sign is fixed to the post with screws.

s.defn: Not subject to change; set in advance and unlikely to be altered.
ex: The fixed price prevents price changes during the sale.
We have a fixed schedule for science projects.

s.defn: Repaired; made to work again after being damaged or broken.
ex: The fixed faucet was repaired by the plumber.
The fixed printer works again after service.

s.defn: To repair or mend something that is broken or not functioning.
ex: During the science project the student fixed the broken telescope.
The technician fixed the faulty sensor to collect accurate data.

s.defn: To fasten or attach something in place so that it stays secure.
ex: The lid was fixed with a screw to keep it closed.
The sign was fixed securely to the wall.

s.defn: To set or arrange something in advance, such as a date or schedule.
ex: They fixed the date for the science fair next month.
The committee fixed the deadline for submissions.

s.defn: To prepare or cook a meal.
ex: Mom fixed a simple lunch for the study group.
We fixed a quick dinner before the math lesson.

s.defn: A level of quality or attainment used as a benchmark to judge something.
ex: The school sets a high standard for writing.
Researchers compare results to the standard set by guidelines.

s.defn: A flag or banner used to symbolize a group, authority, or country.
ex: The royal standard waved over the castle.
The regiment carried its standard into battle.

s.defn: usual or typical; commonly used in ordinary settings.
ex: In math class students use the standard method to solve problems.
The science lab follows the standard procedure for safety checks.

s.defn: conforming to defined rules or a required level; meeting a standard.
ex: The school ensures every assignment meets the standard of clarity.
A standard grade indicates the work is on the expected level.

s.defn: A sign or cue that conveys information about a situation or outcome.
ex: The flag raised at noon is a signal to begin class.
A rising grade on the test acts as a signal that understanding grows.

s.defn: A device that conveys information by emitting light, sound, or other signals.
ex: Solar lights function as a signal device for warning.
A loud alarm is an emergency signal to evacuate.

s.defn: In data analysis, a detectable pattern that stands out from background noise and carries information.
ex: Researchers try to separate the signal from the noise in the data.
A clear signal shows the trend despite random fluctuations.

s.defn: To convey information or a message to others by signs or actions.
ex: The teacher signaled understanding with a nod.
A green light signals that the crossing is safe.

s.defn: To prompt or guide someone to take a course of action by a sign or cue.
ex: The coach signaled the players to start.
The teacher signaled the class to quiet down.

s.defn: To indicate the status or presence of something via a device or indicator.
ex: The warning light signals an error on the panel.
The beeping sound signals low battery.

s.defn: easily seen or noticed; obvious or important; standing out in a way that attracts attention.
ex: The data showed a signal improvement in test scores.
The chart revealed a signal difference between groups.

s.defn: relating to or used to convey a signal; designed to indicate or transmit information.
ex: The red light is a signal cue indicating when to stop.
A clear signal indicating the system status was recorded in logs.

s.defn: The brightness or gleam on a surface produced by reflection of light.
ex: The polished maple floor shows a bright shine under the gymnasium lights.
A consistent shine on the polished wood in the classroom demonstrates careful maintenance.

s.defn: To emit light or reflect light so that something is bright and visible.
ex: The sun shines on the field in the morning.
The lantern shines across the room during a power outage.

s.defn: To perform very well or to stand out by achievement or skill.
ex: The student shined in the science fair.
She shined in the class presentation.

s.defn: A statement that forecasts a future observation or outcome based on scientific evidence or a model.
ex: The prediction said the ice would melt faster in warm water than in cold water.
Scientists use a prediction from a model to plan measurements in the field.

s.defn: A measurable outcome stated before an experiment that will test a hypothesis.
ex: Our prediction before the experiment was that the plant would grow taller with more light.
Students state a prediction to decide what data the experiment should collect.

s.defn: A numerical estimate produced by a scientific model that predicts a measured quantity.
ex: The model prediction for pond temperature was fifteen degrees Celsius on Monday.
Researchers compare the prediction to the measured temperature to check the model.
